stem: A 46-year-old woman attends the gynaecology outpatient clinic of a regional hospital, where the visiting gynaecologist reviews patients by phone between monthly visits. She has had irregular periods for a year and assumed she was perimenopausal, but now has seven weeks of amenorrhoea, light spotting and three days of mild left iliac fossa discomfort. She is haemodynamically stable (heart rate 78/min, blood pressure 124/78 mmHg) with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no peritonism. Serum beta-hCG is 1,800 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound this morning shows an empty uterus, a 2.5 cm left adnexal mass without a yolk sac or fetal cardiac activity, and a small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Liver and renal function and full blood count are normal. She lives on a station 250 km away, has no car this week and says she cannot return for blood tests until the next clinic in a month. The gynaecologist is considering methotrexate.
lead_in: Which feature makes medical management with methotrexate unsuitable for her?

options.text: A serum beta-hCG of 1,800 IU/L
A small amount of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas
Her inability to return for serial beta-hCG monitoring
An adnexal mass of 2.5 cm without fetal cardiac activity

explanations.A: A beta-hCG of 1,800 IU/L is well below the level (around 5,000 IU/L) above which methotrexate failure becomes likely; a low hCG favours medical management.
explanations.B: A small volume of free pelvic fluid is common in unruptured ectopic pregnancy and, in a stable woman without peritonism, does not by itself indicate rupture or exclude methotrexate; a large haemoperitoneum or haemodynamic instability would.
explanations.C: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy requires serum beta-hCG on days 4 and 7 and then weekly until undetectable, plus ready access to emergency care if rupture occurs. A woman who cannot attend this follow-up or reach hospital quickly is not a candidate, and surgical management should be discussed with her instead.
explanations.D: A mass under 3.5 cm with no fetal cardiac activity is within the usual criteria for methotrexate; a larger mass or cardiac activity would be reasons to prefer surgery.

learning_point: Methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy is only safe when the woman is stable, has a low beta-hCG and a small mass without cardiac activity, and can reliably return for serial beta-hCG monitoring and urgent care.
setting_note: In a regional hospital, distance and transport often decide between medical and surgical management: a woman who cannot return for day 4 and 7 bloods or reach an operating theatre quickly if she ruptures should be discussed with the gynaecologist for laparoscopy, either locally when the visiting surgeon is available or in Adelaide.

generation.uncertainty_note: Exact hCG and mass-size cut-offs for methotrexate vary between guidelines (3,500 to 5,000 IU/L; 3.5 to 4 cm); the item avoids hinging on a specific numeric cut-off.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health
references.locator: Ectopic pregnancy: medical management with methotrexate, patient selection and follow-up

references.title: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Early pregnancy loss
references.locator: Ectopic pregnancy: criteria for methotrexate and follow-up

tutor_context: Key facts: methotrexate is for stable women with unruptured ectopic, hCG usually under 5,000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, normal FBC/LFT/UEC and reliable follow-up (hCG day 4 and 7, then weekly). Misconceptions: any free fluid means rupture; age alone is a contraindication. Out of scope: methotrexate dosing and the decision itself, which belong to the gynaecologist.
plan: Tests recall of patient-selection criteria for methotrexate in ectopic pregnancy, evidencing 4.1 and 1.7. A perimenopausal woman in a regional clinic with an unruptured ectopic makes the follow-up constraint real. Distractors are features interns misread as contraindications (small free fluid, hCG level, mass size). Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines and the Queensland early pregnancy loss guideline.

stem: A 22-year-old woman sees you in a general practice attached to a metropolitan general hospital. Her last period was six weeks ago and a home pregnancy test yesterday was positive. For 24 hours she has had intermittent right iliac fossa pain, worse this morning, and a small amount of brown vaginal spotting. She had chlamydia treated two years ago. She looks well: heart rate 86/min, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, afebrile. Abdominal examination shows mild right iliac fossa tenderness without guarding or rebound. A urine pregnancy test in the practice is positive. She asks whether she can wait and see, because the pain has eased with paracetamol and she has work tomorrow. The practice has no ultrasound; the hospital runs an early pregnancy assessment service and has an emergency department.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a pelvic ultrasound through a community radiology practice for later in the week and review the report when it arrives
Refer her today to the hospital early pregnancy assessment service for serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound
Request serum beta-hCG and progesterone through community pathology and review her tomorrow with the results
Prescribe regular paracetamol and repeat the urine pregnancy test in one week if the pain persists

explanations.A: An ultrasound in several days leaves a possible ectopic pregnancy undiagnosed during the period when it may rupture; the scan should be transvaginal and performed the same day, which community practices often cannot provide.
explanations.B: Any woman with a positive pregnancy test, abdominal pain and bleeding has a possible ectopic pregnancy until an intrauterine pregnancy is seen. Previous chlamydia increases her risk. Same-day serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound through an early pregnancy assessment service, with clear instructions to attend the emergency department if pain worsens or she feels faint, is the standard of care even when she looks well.
explanations.C: A serum beta-hCG alone cannot locate the pregnancy, and a single progesterone does not exclude ectopic pregnancy; waiting a day for results delays definitive imaging.
explanations.D: Analgesia and watchful waiting for a week risks rupture and haemorrhage; pain easing with paracetamol does not exclude an ectopic pregnancy.

learning_point: Pain or bleeding in early pregnancy requires same-day serum beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound to locate the pregnancy, regardless of how well the woman looks.
setting_note: In a regional centre without same-day ultrasound, phone the on-call obstetric or gynaecology team and arrange an urgent scan or transfer the same day; give clear instructions to present to the nearest emergency department immediately if pain increases, she feels faint or bleeding becomes heavy.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and reproductive health
references.locator: Ectopic pregnancy: presentation and diagnosis

references.title: Queensland Clinical Guideline: Early pregnancy loss
references.locator: Assessment of pain and bleeding in early pregnancy; pregnancy of unknown location

tutor_context: Key facts: positive pregnancy test plus pain or bleeding equals possible ectopic until an intrauterine pregnancy is seen; same-day beta-hCG and transvaginal ultrasound; risk factors include previous pelvic infection, tubal surgery, IUD, IVF. Misconceptions: a stable, well-looking woman can wait; a single hCG or progesterone is diagnostic. Out of scope: interpretation of serial hCG trends and choice of treatment.
plan: Tests the management decision that early pregnancy pain and bleeding need same-day hospital-based assessment (4.1, 1.7). A general practice setting with a stable young woman who wants to wait creates the temptation to defer. Distractors are the delays an intern might accept: outpatient scan, community bloods, watchful waiting. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines and the Queensland early pregnancy loss guideline.

stem: A 45-year-old woman at 35 weeks of gestation attends her general practitioner for a routine shared-care antenatal visit; the practice is linked to a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. This is an IVF pregnancy using a donor egg. Her booking blood pressure was 112/70 mmHg and her antenatal course has been uncomplicated. Today her blood pressure is 142/92 mmHg and, after ten minutes of rest, 144/90 mmHg. Urine dipstick shows no protein. She mentions two days of epigastric discomfort and nausea that she has attributed to reflux, with no headache or visual symptoms. Fetal movements are normal and the fundal height is appropriate. She has no oedema. Her next hospital clinic appointment is in two weeks.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe an antacid for reflux and recheck her blood pressure at a nurse visit in one week
Start labetalol 100 mg twice daily and review her blood pressure and a urine protein-creatinine ratio in one week
Request full blood count, liver and renal function and urine protein-creatinine ratio through community pathology and review the results tomorrow
Refer her the same day to the hospital maternity assessment unit for pre-eclampsia investigations and fetal assessment

explanations.A: Treating her as reflux ignores new hypertension after 20 weeks combined with epigastric pain, a recognised warning symptom of pre-eclampsia and HELLP syndrome; waiting a week is unsafe.
explanations.B: Antihypertensive treatment may be needed, but starting it in general practice without investigating for pre-eclampsia delays diagnosis; the blood pressure is only mildly raised, and the concerning feature is the epigastric pain.
explanations.C: These are the right investigations but the wrong timeframe: community pathology results take hours to a day, there is no fetal assessment, and a woman with possible pre-eclampsia and epigastric pain should be assessed in hospital today.
explanations.D: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks must be assessed for pre-eclampsia, which can occur without proteinuria. Epigastric pain with new hypertension is a red flag for hepatic involvement, so same-day hospital assessment with blood tests, urine protein-creatinine ratio and fetal monitoring is required, with the obstetric team deciding on antihypertensives and timing of birth.

learning_point: Epigastric pain with new hypertension in the second half of pregnancy is a pre-eclampsia red flag that needs same-day hospital assessment even when proteinuria is absent and the blood pressure rise is mild.
setting_note: From a regional practice, phone the on-call obstetric team at the nearest birthing hospital and arrange same-day assessment there or transfer; if blood pressure reaches 160/110 mmHg or she develops severe symptoms, she should travel by ambulance.

references.title: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023
references.locator: Definition and diagnosis of pre-eclampsia; assessment of new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks; warning symptoms

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Hypertension in pregnancy: assessment and when to refer

tutor_context: Key facts: hypertension in pregnancy is 140/90 mmHg or above on repeated measurement after 20 weeks; pre-eclampsia is hypertension plus any maternal organ involvement (renal, hepatic, haematological, neurological) or fetal growth restriction, and proteinuria is no longer required; epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, headache, visual disturbance and reduced fetal movements are warning symptoms. Misconceptions: no proteinuria means no pre-eclampsia; mild blood pressure means low urgency. Out of scope: choice and dose of antihypertensive, magnesium sulfate and timing of birth.
plan: Tests recognition that mild new hypertension with epigastric pain is a pre-eclampsia red flag needing same-day hospital assessment (4.1, 1.7). An older IVF pregnancy in shared care sets up the temptation to manage in general practice. Distractors are plausible slower pathways: treat reflux, start an antihypertensive, order the right bloods through community pathology. Supported by the SOMANZ 2023 guideline and Therapeutic Guidelines.

stem: A 23-year-old woman attends the outpatient clinic of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, five days after an uncomplicated vaginal birth at the regional maternity unit. She has felt feverish and shivery for 24 hours, with lower abdominal cramping and offensive-smelling lochia. She is breastfeeding and her breasts are soft and non-tender. Her perineum is intact. Observations: temperature 38.6 °C, heart rate 108/min, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, oxygen saturation 98%. The uterus is tender and slightly bulky on abdominal palpation; there is no loin tenderness. Urine dipstick shows a trace of leucocytes. She has no drug allergies. The GP obstetrician is on call by phone and the hospital has a small inpatient ward.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit her for blood cultures and intravenous amoxicillin, gentamicin and metronidazole
Prescribe oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid and arrange review in the clinic in 48 hours
Prescribe oral cefalexin for a urinary tract infection and send a midstream urine for culture
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to look for retained products before deciding on antibiotics

explanations.A: Fever, uterine tenderness and offensive lochia five days postpartum indicate endometritis. With a temperature of 38.6 °C and tachycardia she has systemic features and should be admitted for blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics covering aerobes and anaerobes, as Therapeutic Guidelines recommends for postpartum endometritis; the GP obstetrician should be informed. Gentamicin and metronidazole are compatible with breastfeeding.
explanations.B: Oral amoxicillin and clavulanic acid is reasonable for mild endometritis in a well woman with low-grade fever who can be reviewed, but her tachycardia and high fever place her outside that group and a 48-hour gap risks progression to sepsis.
explanations.C: A trace of leucocytes on dipstick is common postpartum and does not explain uterine tenderness and offensive lochia; treating for a urinary infection misses the diagnosis and under-treats her.
explanations.D: Ultrasound may be considered later if she fails to improve, but imaging should not delay antibiotics in a febrile, tachycardic postpartum woman.

learning_point: Postpartum fever with uterine tenderness and offensive lochia is endometritis; systemic features such as fever above 38 °C with tachycardia mean admission, blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics rather than oral treatment and outpatient review.
setting_note: In a rural hospital with one junior doctor overnight, admit her early rather than relying on review in 48 hours, phone the GP obstetrician on call, and apply the local deteriorating-patient criteria; if she meets sepsis criteria or does not improve within 24 to 48 hours, discuss transfer to the regional maternity unit or Adelaide.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic
references.locator: Postpartum endometritis: intravenous regimen for moderate to severe infection; oral regimen for mild infection

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Gentamicin and metronidazole: use in breastfeeding

tutor_context: Key facts: endometritis is the commonest cause of postpartum fever after day 2; diagnosis is clinical (fever, uterine tenderness, offensive lochia); intravenous amoxicillin or ampicillin plus gentamicin plus metronidazole for systemic illness, oral amoxicillin-clavulanate for mild cases; also consider mastitis, urinary infection, wound infection, venous thromboembolism. Misconceptions: breastfeeding precludes gentamicin or metronidazole; imaging is needed before treating. Out of scope: management of retained products and surgical evacuation.
plan: Tests the decision between oral outpatient and inpatient intravenous treatment of postpartum endometritis (4.1, 1.7, 1.8). A young breastfeeding woman in a rural outpatient clinic with systemic features makes the choice consequential. Distractors are the oral option that suits milder cases, misattribution to urinary infection, and imaging before antibiotics. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic and the AMH.

stem: A 45-year-old woman at 30 weeks of gestation presents at 2200 to the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital with two days of swelling and aching in her left calf, which is now painful to walk on. She has no chest pain or breathlessness. She has a singleton pregnancy conceived by IVF and a body mass index of 34. Observations: heart rate 92/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, afebrile. The left calf is 4 cm larger in circumference than the right, warm and tender along the medial calf. The ultrasound department does not open until 0800 and the obstetric registrar is on site.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a D-dimer and, if it is below the laboratory threshold, discharge her with antenatal clinic review
Start therapeutic enoxaparin now and arrange compression ultrasound of the leg when imaging opens
Start warfarin tonight and arrange compression ultrasound of the leg as an outpatient
Advise compression stockings, elevation and analgesia, with review in the antenatal clinic in one week

explanations.A: D-dimer rises physiologically in pregnancy, so a positive result is uninterpretable, and a negative result is not validated to exclude deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy; it should not guide discharge.
explanations.B: Pregnancy, IVF and obesity are risk factors, and unilateral calf swelling with a 4 cm difference makes deep vein thrombosis likely. Because imaging is delayed, therapeutic weight-based low-molecular-weight heparin should be started now and compression ultrasound performed when available; enoxaparin does not cross the placenta and is the anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy. The obstetric registrar should be informed.
explanations.C: Warfarin crosses the placenta, is teratogenic and is associated with fetal haemorrhage; it is not used for venous thromboembolism in pregnancy, and outpatient imaging delays confirmation.
explanations.D: Conservative measures alone leave a probable deep vein thrombosis untreated for a week, risking extension and pulmonary embolism.

learning_point: Suspected deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy is treated with weight-based therapeutic low-molecular-weight heparin while awaiting compression ultrasound, and D-dimer should not be used to exclude it.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without overnight ultrasound, the same approach applies: start enoxaparin after discussing with the obstetric team on call and arrange imaging the next morning locally or in Adelaide; if she develops chest pain or breathlessness, treat as possible pulmonary embolism and arrange urgent transfer.
presentation: pregnant patient in the emergency department

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular
references.locator: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy: diagnosis and treatment with low-molecular-weight heparin

references.title: SOMANZ and ASTH consensus: Recommendations for the diagnosis and treatment of deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism in pregnancy and the postpartum period
references.locator: Diagnostic approach; role of D-dimer; empirical anticoagulation when imaging delayed

tutor_context: Key facts: pregnancy increases venous thromboembolism risk four- to five-fold; left leg is more often affected; compression ultrasound is the first-line test; therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily (or 1.5 mg/kg daily) based on current weight; warfarin and direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in pregnancy. Misconceptions: a negative D-dimer excludes clot in pregnancy; anticoagulation must wait for imaging. Out of scope: management of pulmonary embolism, imaging choice for suspected PE, peripartum anticoagulation planning.
plan: Tests the management of suspected deep vein thrombosis in pregnancy when imaging is delayed (4.1, 1.7, 1.8). An older, obese IVF pregnancy at night in a general hospital makes the choice between empirical heparin and waiting realistic. Distractors are the D-dimer trap, warfarin, and conservative measures. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines and the SOMANZ/ASTH consensus.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is seen in the outpatient clinic of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, referred by the practice nurse after a positive pregnancy test. By dates she is six weeks pregnant; the pregnancy is unplanned but wanted. Her medications are perindopril 5 mg daily for hypertension started two years ago, sodium valproate 500 mg twice daily for generalised epilepsy (seizure-free for three years), sertraline 50 mg daily for anxiety, and folic acid 0.5 mg daily that she started last week. Her blood pressure today is 128/80 mmHg. Her neurologist is in Adelaide and sees her annually; the GP obstetrician is available by phone. You are the PGY2 resident running the clinic.
lead_in: Which action should you take before she leaves the clinic today?

options.text: Cease perindopril today and ask the GP obstetrician whether an alternative antihypertensive is needed
Cease sodium valproate today and request an urgent appointment with her neurologist in Adelaide
Change sertraline to a different antidepressant with more pregnancy safety data and review in two weeks
Replace sodium valproate with lamotrigine today and arrange an urgent neurology review

explanations.A: ACE inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetotoxicity (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, fetal death), and should be stopped as soon as pregnancy is confirmed. Her blood pressure today is 128/80 mmHg so she may need nothing for now; the GP obstetrician should decide whether labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa is required. This is within a resident's scope and must happen today.
explanations.B: Sodium valproate carries the highest teratogenic risk of the antiepileptic drugs and her neurologist should be contacted urgently this week, but abrupt cessation risks breakthrough seizures that endanger her and the pregnancy. Antiepileptic changes in pregnancy are specialist decisions.
explanations.C: Sertraline is one of the better-studied antidepressants in pregnancy and is usually continued; switching risks relapse and offers no safety benefit.
explanations.D: Lamotrigine is a safer antiepileptic in pregnancy, but a switch requires slow cross-titration under neurologist supervision with monitoring of levels; a resident substituting it in clinic is unsafe and outside scope.

learning_point: When pregnancy is confirmed in a woman on an ACE inhibitor, stop it the same day and arrange a safe alternative if needed; antiepileptic drugs are never stopped or swapped abruptly and need urgent specialist input, with folic acid increased to 5 mg daily.
setting_note: In a rural clinic the urgent specialist phone calls are part of the same day's work: the GP obstetrician for antihypertensive choice and shared-care antenatal planning, and the neurologist's rooms in Adelaide or the on-call neurology registrar for an expedited valproate review. Increase folic acid to 5 mg daily today because she is on valproate.

generation.uncertainty_note: AMH and the TGA advise ceasing ACE inhibitors at confirmation of pregnancy; data on first-trimester malformation risk are mixed, but cessation itself is uncontroversial. High-dose folic acid is also a same-day action and is addressed in the learning point and setting note rather than as an option.

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Perindopril and ACE inhibitors: pregnancy (contraindicated); Antiepileptics: pregnancy and valproate

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology
references.locator: Epilepsy: management in pregnancy; do not stop antiepileptic therapy abruptly

tutor_context: Key facts: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are stopped at confirmation of pregnancy and replaced with labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa if needed; valproate is the most teratogenic antiepileptic but must not be stopped or swapped abruptly; women on valproate need folic acid 5 mg daily; sertraline is generally continued. Misconceptions: stopping valproate immediately protects the fetus; sertraline must be changed. Out of scope: antiepileptic cross-titration regimens and pregnancy category labelling details.
plan: Tests prioritisation of medication changes at pregnancy confirmation: which action is urgent and within a resident's scope versus which needs a specialist (4.1, 1.7, 1.8). A rural clinic with specialists by phone makes scope and sequencing matter. Distractors are the tempting but unsafe immediate valproate changes and an unnecessary sertraline switch. Supported by the AMH and Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology.

stem: You are the evening cover resident at a large metropolitan teaching hospital. At 2130 a nurse asks you to review a 79-year-old woman with severe COPD on home oxygen, admitted two days ago with pneumonia. Her respiratory rate is 32/min, oxygen saturation 86% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, heart rate 118/min and blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, and she is drowsy but rousable, meeting rapid response criteria. The nurse shows you a certified Advance Care Directive in the notes: she refuses intubation and CPR in any circumstances, but wants treatments that may get her home, including a trial of mask ventilation. No Resuscitation Plan (7-Step Pathway) has been completed by the day team. Her husband, her substitute decision-maker, is not contactable yet. The medical registrar is in the emergency department.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Activate a rapid response call and proceed with full escalation, including intubation if required, because no Resuscitation Plan has been completed
Withhold further active treatment and start end-of-life comfort care, in keeping with the limits in her directive
Activate a rapid response call and treat within her directive's limits, including non-invasive ventilation
Defer treatment decisions until her husband can be reached to give consent as her substitute decision-maker

explanations.A: Under the Advance Care Directives Act 2013 (SA), a binding refusal of CPR or intubation in a certified directive must be followed when it applies to the current circumstances; a missing Resuscitation Plan does not override it. Intubating her against her refusal would be unlawful.
explanations.B: Her directive refuses only intubation and CPR; it explicitly asks for treatment that might get her home. Withholding controlled oxygen, antibiotics, bronchodilators and non-invasive ventilation misreads a limitation of treatment as a request for palliation.
explanations.C: She is deteriorating and meets escalation criteria, so the rapid response team should be called now. Her directive sets the ceiling of care (no intubation or CPR) and permits a trial of non-invasive ventilation, so treatment proceeds within those limits. The registrar should document a Resuscitation Plan reflecting the directive, and the husband should be updated when reached.
explanations.D: A substitute decision-maker cannot override a binding refusal, and his consent is not needed for treatment she has asked for; delaying escalation while he is contacted risks avoidable harm.

learning_point: A certified Advance Care Directive sets the ceiling of treatment, not the floor: a refusal of intubation and CPR is binding and does not prevent active escalation of everything else the patient wants.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without on-site intensive care, the same ceiling applies; non-invasive ventilation may be available in the emergency department or ward, and the directive informs whether retrieval to Adelaide for higher-level care is appropriate, which should be discussed with the on-call physician.
secondary_areas: Palliative care and goals of care

references.title: Advance Care Directives Act 2013 (SA): information for health practitioners
references.locator: Binding and non-binding provisions; when a refusal of health care must be followed; role of substitute decision-makers

references.title: SA Health Resuscitation Planning: 7 Step Pathway policy directive
references.locator: Documenting a Resuscitation Plan consistent with an Advance Care Directive; care within agreed limits

tutor_context: Key facts: in SA a certified Advance Care Directive's refusal of specific treatment is binding when the person lacks capacity and the refusal applies to the circumstances; other provisions are wishes that guide care; a substitute decision-maker cannot consent to treatment the person has refused; a Resuscitation Plan is the clinical order that translates the directive into bedside instructions. Misconceptions: no Resuscitation Plan means full resuscitation regardless; a directive means do nothing. Out of scope: resolving disputes between family and directive, and the technical delivery of non-invasive ventilation.
plan: Tests applying an Advance Care Directive to an acute deterioration after hours (1.4, 3.2, 1.9). A woman with severe COPD and a directive that refuses intubation but requests a trial of mask ventilation makes the ceiling-of-care distinction necessary. Distractors are the two misreadings of the directive and deferring to the absent husband. Supported by SA Health guidance on the ACD Act and the 7 Step Pathway.

stem: A 68-year-old man is admitted to the surgical ward of a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North the afternoon before an elective inguinal hernia repair by the visiting surgeon. He is independent, has well-controlled type 2 diabetes and is otherwise well. While you are clerking him he hands you a copy of his Advance Care Directive, completed last year after his wife's death. It states that he refuses CPR and life support 'if I am dying from an illness that cannot be cured and will not recover a meaningful quality of life'. He has not discussed it with the surgeon. The nurse asks whether she should write 'not for CPR' on his chart and whether the anaesthetist needs to know.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Record 'not for resuscitation' on his observation chart tonight because his directive refuses CPR
Return the directive to him and explain that it does not apply while he has decision-making capacity
Ask the visiting surgeon to override the directive before he goes to theatre tomorrow morning
Clarify his perioperative wishes with him, tell the surgeon and anaesthetist, and document a Resuscitation Plan

explanations.A: His refusal is conditional on dying from an incurable illness without prospect of recovery; a reversible anaesthetic or surgical complication in a well man does not meet that condition, so a blanket not-for-CPR order misapplies the directive and could cost him his life.
explanations.B: The directive only takes effect if he loses capacity, but it is still relevant information that must be filed, flagged and considered; dismissing it discourages him from raising his wishes and leaves the team unprepared.
explanations.C: A directive is the patient's own expression of wishes and cannot be overridden by a surgeon; the right step is to clarify it with the patient, not to seek to set it aside.
explanations.D: The binding provisions of a directive apply only in the circumstances the person described and only once they have lost capacity. The intern should clarify with him, while he has capacity, what he would want if a potentially reversible complication occurred in theatre, place the directive in the notes, alert the surgeon and anaesthetist, and ensure a Resuscitation Plan (7 Step Pathway) is completed that reflects his wishes.

learning_point: An Advance Care Directive's refusals apply only in the circumstances it describes and once capacity is lost, so a well patient before elective surgery should be asked directly what he wants perioperatively and the team informed.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the visiting surgeon and anaesthetist may arrive the morning of the list, so the conversation and documentation should be done the afternoon before and handed over explicitly; if the patient's wishes are unclear, the on-call physician can help before theatre.

references.title: Advance Care Directives Act 2013 (SA): information for health practitioners
references.locator: When binding refusals apply; relevance of capacity; health practitioner obligations

references.title: SA Health Resuscitation Planning: 7 Step Pathway policy directive
references.locator: Completing a Resuscitation Plan with the patient before a procedure

tutor_context: Key facts: a directive speaks for the person only when they cannot; binding refusals apply only in the circumstances described; perioperative resuscitation wishes should be discussed explicitly with a patient who has capacity and documented in a Resuscitation Plan that the anaesthetist and surgeon see. Misconceptions: any mention of CPR refusal means not-for-resuscitation; directives are irrelevant while the patient can speak. Out of scope: anaesthetic-specific consent for suspension of limitations during surgery.
plan: Tests how an intern handles a directive presented by a capable patient before elective surgery (1.4, 3.2, 1.2). A regional surgical ward with a visiting surgeon makes timely handover of the conversation important. Distractors are the blanket not-for-CPR order, dismissing the directive, and asking the surgeon to override it. Supported by SA Health ACD Act guidance and the 7 Step Pathway.

stem: An 88-year-old woman on the surgical ward of a metropolitan teaching hospital is three days post repair of a fractured neck of femur. She is taking oxycodone immediate-release 2.5 mg four times a day for pain, regular paracetamol, and her usual amlodipine and pantoprazole. She has not opened her bowels since admission five days ago and reports bloating and discomfort. Her abdomen is soft and mildly distended with normal bowel sounds; rectal examination shows soft stool in the rectum. She is eating small meals, drinking about 800 mL a day, and mobilises only short distances with physiotherapy. She has no history of bowel obstruction, is not vomiting, and has normal renal function. No laxative was charted on admission.
lead_in: Which laxative is most appropriate to prescribe?

options.text: Psyllium husk 3.5 g twice daily in water
Docusate with senna 2 tablets nocte
Liquid paraffin 15 mL at night
Methylnaltrexone 8 mg subcutaneously daily

explanations.A: Bulk-forming laxatives need a good fluid intake and mobility to work; in an immobile older patient drinking under a litre a day and taking opioids they can worsen distension and cause impaction.
explanations.B: Opioid-induced constipation responds to a stimulant laxative, usually combined with a softener, taken regularly rather than as needed. Docusate with senna is the standard first-line choice in Therapeutic Guidelines and should be charted whenever an opioid is prescribed for more than a day or two in an older person.
explanations.C: Liquid paraffin carries a risk of aspiration lipoid pneumonia in older or frail patients and interferes with absorption of fat-soluble vitamins; it is not recommended.
explanations.D: Methylnaltrexone, a peripherally acting opioid antagonist, is reserved for opioid-induced constipation that has failed conventional laxatives, usually in palliative care; it is not first line.

learning_point: A regular stimulant laxative such as senna with docusate should be charted alongside any opioid for an older inpatient; bulk-forming agents are unsuitable when fluid intake and mobility are poor.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal
references.locator: Constipation in adults: opioid-induced constipation; choice of laxative

tutor_context: Key facts: prescribe a regular stimulant laxative (senna) with or without a softener (docusate) whenever starting an opioid; osmotic laxatives (macrogol, lactulose) are acceptable alternatives or add-ons; bulk-forming agents need fluid and mobility; liquid paraffin is avoided in older people; methylnaltrexone is for refractory opioid-induced constipation. Misconceptions: fibre supplements are the gentlest first choice for everyone; laxatives should be as-needed only. Out of scope: management of faecal impaction and bowel obstruction.
plan: Tests recall of first-line laxative choice for opioid-induced constipation in an older inpatient (1.4, 3.2, 1.8). A post-hip-fracture woman on oxycodone with no laxative charted is the everyday scenario. Distractors are the bulk-forming agent interns reach for, liquid paraffin, and a second-line agent. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal and the AMH.

stem: You are the evening cover intern at a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. At 2000 a nurse phones about an 81-year-old woman admitted yesterday with a urinary tract infection. She lives independently, drives, and had no confusion on admission. She is now pulling at her intravenous cannula, trying to climb over the bed rails and insisting she needs to get to the bus stop, and she does not know where she is. She has refused her evening medications. Her last observations two hours ago were heart rate 96/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, temperature 37.6 °C and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Her chart includes intravenous ceftriaxone, oxycodone 5 mg as needed (given twice today for back pain) and temazepam 10 mg at night, started on admission. The nurse asks you to chart something to settle her.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Chart olanzapine 5 mg wafer as needed over the phone so the nurse can give a dose now and reassess later
Chart an additional dose of temazepam 10 mg tonight to help her settle and sleep through
Attend now to assess for pain, retention, hypoxia and medication causes, and start non-pharmacological measures
Request an urgent CT brain tonight to exclude a stroke as the cause of her new confusion and agitation

explanations.A: Antipsychotics for delirium are reserved for severe distress or imminent danger when non-drug measures have failed, and only after the patient has been assessed; prescribing by phone without examination risks oversedation, falls and masking a deteriorating cause.
explanations.B: Benzodiazepines worsen and prolong delirium in older people and increase falls; the temazepam started on admission is itself a likely contributor and should be ceased, not increased.
explanations.C: This is new acute confusion with inattention in a previously independent woman: delirium. The intern should attend, repeat observations, check a blood glucose and bladder scan, assess pain and bowels, review the medication chart (oxycodone and temazepam are likely contributors) and ask the nurses to implement reorientation, lighting, hearing aids and glasses, and family presence, as set out in the Delirium Clinical Care Standard.
explanations.D: Imaging is indicated if there are focal neurological signs, a head injury, or anticoagulation and a fall; with an obvious precipitant (infection, opioid, benzodiazepine) and no focal signs, a CT is not the first step.

learning_point: Acute confusion in an older inpatient is delirium until proven otherwise: assess in person for precipitants and treat them, use non-pharmacological measures first, and never prescribe sedatives over the phone.

references.title: Delirium Clinical Care Standard (2021)
references.locator: Quality statements 3 to 6: assessment, identifying and treating causes, non-pharmacological interventions, minimising antipsychotic use

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
